clinicalPearls: Defined by the coexistence of a papular naevus spilus (speckled lentiginous naevus) with an organoid naevus sebaceus or epidermal naevus in the same patient
Regarded as an example of twin spotting (didymosis), where two mosaic clones arise from a single post-zygotic event
Post-zygotic activating HRAS variants have been identified, linking it to the naevus sebaceus and Schimmelpenning spectrum
Extracutaneous features may include neurological abnormalities such as seizures and developmental delay
Ocular and skeletal anomalies, and segmental sensory or motor disturbance (dysaesthesia, muscular weakness) may accompany the cutaneous lesions
Hemihypertrophy and hypophosphataemic (vitamin-D-resistant) rickets are recognised systemic associations
Management is generic and multidisciplinary: surveillance of the naevi, antiseizure therapy where needed, and correction of any hypophosphataemic rickets
reference.pathophysiology: Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica is understood as a form of twin spotting, in which a single post-zygotic somatic recombination event produces two genetically distinct daughter clones side by side, one giving rise to a pigmentary papular naevus spilus and the other to an organoid naevus sebaceus or epidermal naevus. Activating HRAS variants in the RAS-MAPK pathway have been implicated, which is why the condition overlaps mechanistically with naevus sebaceus and Schimmelpenning syndrome. When the mosaic clones also involve neuroectodermal, ocular and mesodermal tissue, the associated neurological, ocular and skeletal anomalies, hemihypertrophy and FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemic rickets develop.
additionalInvestigations: Skin examination and biopsy to characterise both naevus components
MRI of the brain where neurological features are present
Serum phosphate and skeletal survey to detect hypophosphataemic rickets and hemihypertrophy
Neurological evaluation of any segmental sensory or motor disturbance
Molecular testing of lesional tissue for HRAS variants where available
redFlags: Progressive neurological deficit or segmental weakness
Suspicious change within the melanocytic or organoid naevus
Unexplained bone pain or fractures suggesting hypophosphataemic rickets
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent of extracutaneous involvement; limited cutaneous disease has a good outlook, whereas neurological, skeletal or metabolic complications increase morbidity and require ongoing multidisciplinary management.
pitfalls: Regarding the two naevi as coincidental rather than recognising the twin-spotting syndrome
Missing treatable hypophosphataemic rickets as a cause of skeletal symptoms
Overlooking segmental sensory or motor disturbance as part of the condition
Failing to arrange neuroimaging when neurological features are present
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: No curative therapy exists, so management is directed at the individual manifestations across affected systems
Dermatological management of the naevus sebaceus or epidermal naevus and the naevus spilus, with excision of symptomatic or suspicious lesions given the risk of secondary neoplasms
Correction of FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemic rickets with oral phosphate and active vitamin D analogues, and anti-FGF23 antibody therapy where appropriate, monitoring phosphate and renal function
Antiepileptic therapy and neurological management of seizures and developmental delay
Ophthalmological assessment and treatment of ocular anomalies, and orthopaedic management of skeletal anomalies, hemihypertrophy and segmental sensory or motor disturbance
Multidisciplinary follow-up across dermatology, neurology, endocrinology and ophthalmology
Genetic counselling explaining the sporadic post-zygotic mosaic HRAS basis and generally low recurrence risk
